name: Landslides
description: Landslides move rock, soil, or debris downhill when a slope loses stability. In Iran, research shows why rainfall, earthquake shaking, and changes to slopes must be considered together rather than treated as isolated causes.

seo.title: Landslides in Iran: Rainfall, Earthquakes and Slope Failure | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran's landslide hazards, how water and earthquakes affect slopes, and what national hazard models can and cannot establish.

content.heading: A hazard with several forms
content.content:
A landslide is downhill movement of rock, soil, or loose debris under gravity. The term covers different processes: a rockfall, a deep failure within a hillside, and a shallow flow of wet debris do not move in the same way. Material, movement, speed, and moisture all matter when describing a failure. The US National Park Service's explanation provides this general physical framework; it is not an inventory of Iranian events. [s1]

The distinction matters when reading reports from Iran. Describing every failure as a mudslide can obscure whether the problem involved falling rock, a moving block of ground, or water-rich material flowing downslope. A useful account identifies the movement and its setting before attributing a cause. [s1]

content.heading: How slopes become unstable
content.content:
Water can weaken a slope by increasing pressure within the spaces between soil particles. Streams can also remove support by eroding the foot of a hillside. Earthquake shaking adds stresses and can initiate movement in ground that was already vulnerable. Human alterations matter too: excavation beneath a slope or additional loading above it changes the balance of forces. These mechanisms explain why a road cutting or developed hillside requires attention to both its shape and its drainage. [s1]

Rainfall and shaking can also interact. An Iran-wide modeling study published in 2024 examined their effects separately and in sequence. Its results indicated that earthquake shaking after heavy precipitation could produce greater modeled landslide hazard than the reverse sequence. This is a finding from a particular analytical framework, not a rule that predicts the outcome on every hillside. [s2]

content.heading: What Iranian case histories establish
content.content:
The study tested its framework against Mela Kabod, associated with the Sarpol-e Zahab earthquake in western Iran in 2017, and Kalpush in northeastern Iran in 2019. Its Kalpush discussion emphasizes prolonged wet conditions as well as individual rainfall episodes. Together, the cases illustrate why slope assessment must consider conditions before the final trigger. A hillside carries a history of wetting, deformation, and disturbance into the next event. [s2]

The authors explicitly describe their national analysis as preliminary and acknowledge limits in predicting local displacement. National modeling can help identify places requiring closer investigation; it cannot establish that a particular building site or road is safe. That distinction also prevents a modeled hazard category from being mistaken for an observed annual landslide count. [s2]

content.title: Different routes toward slope failure
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Rain or snowmelt"] -->|"Can increase pore-water pressure"| B["Reduced slope stability"]
  C["Stream erosion"] -->|"Can remove support at the slope foot"| B
  D["Excavation or added loading"] -->|"Changes the force balance"| B
  E["Earthquake shaking"] -->|"Adds destabilizing stresses"| B
  B -->|"May lead to"| F["Downslope movement"]
```
content.summary: The arrows identify possible physical mechanisms, not inevitable outcomes. Several mechanisms may act on the same slope; the diagram does not assign their relative importance at a particular Iranian site.

content.heading: Reading landslide evidence carefully
content.content: For an international reader, the most useful question is therefore not simply whether a region experiences landslides. It is what material moved, what changed beforehand, and how the explanation was established. Iran's compound-hazard research supports examining rainfall and earthquakes together, while its stated limitations reinforce the need for more detailed local analysis. A national overview is a starting point for understanding the hazard, rather than a substitute for investigating an individual slope. [s2]

name: Dust Storms
description: Dust storms affect Iran through emissions from domestic landscapes and material transported across borders. Their causes connect strong winds with exposed soils, wetland conditions, vegetation, and land and water management.

seo.title: Dust Storms in Iran: Sources, Sistan and Wetland Connections | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore how winds, dry soils, wetlands and cross-border transport shape Iran's dust storms, and distinguish mitigation plans from proven outcomes.

content.heading: Where the dust begins
content.content:
A sand and dust storm begins when strong winds lift particles from exposed dry ground. Dust affecting Iran can originate inside the country or arrive from neighboring countries. The place experiencing poor visibility or airborne particles is therefore not necessarily the place where the material was released. UNDP's Iran factsheet treats both domestic emissions and cross-border transport as essential parts of the problem. [s1]

This makes dust storms a land-management issue as well as a weather phenomenon. Wind supplies the force, but the condition of the surface influences how much material is available. A forecast can help anticipate transport; it does not by itself restore vegetation or resolve the water-management conditions that expose sediments. UNDP consequently links forecasting with land restoration and regional cooperation. [s1]

content.heading: Sistan's distinctive wind regime
content.content:
Sistan, in eastern Iran, illustrates why a single national description is insufficient. The abstract of a satellite-based study describes predominantly northwesterly winds known as the 120-day winds and more frequent dust storms in spring and summer. The researchers examined vegetation, wind, and satellite observations of atmospheric aerosols, meaning particles suspended in the air. Their abstract reports relationships that differ with the timescale of analysis. [s2]

That qualification matters: a seasonal association between wind and dust does not mean that wind alone explains changes between years. The inspected abstract identifies vegetation changes as relevant to interpreting the results. It supports a regional explanation of interacting conditions, but does not provide an inspected annual numerical table suitable for reproduction here. [s2]

content.heading: Why wetland management enters the discussion
content.content:
UNEP connects wetland drying in Iran with water extraction, changes to water bodies, and climate pressures, and identifies increased dust as one consequence of degraded landscapes. Its account of the shared Hawizeh–Haur Al-Azim marshes also shows why environmental management crosses national boundaries. The wetland extends between Iraq and Iran, making cooperation relevant to its conservation and to efforts to reduce dust. [s3]

This relationship should not be simplified into a claim that every dry wetland produces the same dust hazard. The broader lesson is that water allocation and land condition belong in the explanation alongside atmospheric transport. UNEP's account supports the rationale for cooperation; it does not establish that a particular restoration project has already reduced regional dust concentrations. [s3]

content.title: From exposed ground to transported dust
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Dry exposed soil or sediment"] -->|"Provides erodible material"| C["Particle release"]
  B["Strong surface winds"] -->|"Lift available particles"| C
  C -->|"Enters moving air"| D["Atmospheric transport"]
  D -->|"Can cross national boundaries"| E["Downwind exposure"]
  F["Land and water management"] -->|"Can alter surface conditions"| A
```
content.summary: The diagram separates the emitting landscape from the downwind location. It explains possible mechanisms without assigning a fixed domestic or foreign share to dust experienced in Iran.

content.heading: What recent initiatives establish
content.content:
In its August 2026 update, UNDP describes support for identifying priority domestic source areas, strengthening monitoring, and incorporating dust concerns into landscape planning. It also reports work on vegetation restoration, water use, and grazing management in the Touran landscape in Semnan Province. These are documented program activities according to the implementing organization. [s4]

They should be distinguished from independently demonstrated reductions in dust exposure. The update includes systems still planned or under development, alongside reported work already undertaken. Understanding Iran's response therefore requires two separate questions: whether monitoring and restoration measures were implemented, and whether comparable measurements subsequently show lower emissions or exposure. The inspected material supports the direction of the intervention more clearly than its long-term effectiveness. [s4]

name: Human Geography
description: Iran's human geography examines how population, settlements, migration, and infrastructure occupy a varied physical landscape. Census records, metropolitan studies, and the history of water management reveal different aspects of that geography, but require careful attention to dates and boundaries.

seo.title: Iran's Human Geography: Population, Settlements and Migration | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran's settlement patterns, metropolitan growth, migration and water-dependent landscapes, with clear distinctions between historical evidence and current data gaps.

content.heading: Reading the inhabited landscape
content.content:
Human geography asks how people organize life across space: where they settle, how places connect, and why those patterns change. In Iran, physical conditions are part of that explanation. FAO's country profile describes an extensive mountainous and desert landscape, including the Zagros mountain system. These broad conditions provide context, but a physical map alone cannot explain the distribution of jobs, services, or population. [s1]

This branch brings together population distribution, provincial density, rural settlements, border cities, sparsely populated regions, and metropolitan areas. Each uses a different lens. A settlement map shows locations; density relates people to area; migration describes movement; and metropolitan analysis examines connections extending beyond a single municipality. Keeping those questions separate makes the evidence easier to interpret.

content.heading: Begin with a dated population baseline
content.content:
The United Nations Statistics Division reproduces Iran's 2016 census total as 79,926,270 people. The record identifies a de jure census, meaning a count based on usual residence, and marks the figure as final and completely tabulated. This is a historical baseline, not a count of the population at the editorial cutoff. [s2]

Population comparisons also depend on geography. A province, a city within its administrative limits, and a wider metropolitan region describe different territories. The Habitat III national report explicitly distinguishes Tehran's city limits from its surrounding metropolitan region. Its account identifies growth outside the central city's boundaries, demonstrating why a city total cannot stand in for the whole urban region. [s3]

Provincial density requires the same care: population and area must refer to the same boundary definition and date. The present research has not established a complete, comparable provincial table, so no density ranking is supplied.

content.heading: Urbanization has several causes
content.content:
A UNFPA evaluation attributes Iran's urbanization to natural population increase, migration, and growth in the number of cities. This is a useful corrective to the assumption that every increase in urban population represents someone leaving a village. Administrative changes can alter the recorded urban share alongside births, deaths, and movement. [s4]

UNFPA's publication on internal migration also emphasizes varied motives: employment, departure from disadvantaged areas, movement toward urban outskirts, and relocation to places offering a preferred environment. These explanations describe different kinds of movement and should not be compressed into one national story of rural departure. The publication landing page establishes this framing; its full report was not successfully retrieved for detailed verification. [s5]

The historical Habitat III account identifies metropolitan growth beyond Tehran as well, discussing Mashhad, Tabriz, Esfahan, and Shiraz. Its descriptions belong to the reporting period of that document and do not establish current city rankings or present-day population totals. [s3]

content.heading: Water infrastructure as settlement infrastructure
content.content:
Rural geography includes the systems that make permanent settlement possible. UNESCO's account of the Persian Qanat describes underground channels that collect groundwater and convey it by gravity toward agricultural land. An aquifer is a water-bearing underground formation; an alluvial fan is a deposit of sediment spreading outward where a stream leaves higher ground. The relationship between these formations and water collection helps explain settlement in arid landscapes. [s6]

UNESCO connects the distribution of early settlements on the inner plateau's alluvial fans with qanat systems. It also describes associated reservoirs, mills, gardens, and communal management. The significance is both technical and social: a settlement depended on maintaining a channel and organizing access to its water. This heritage evidence explains an important historical pattern, rather than the present condition of every Iranian village. [s6]

content.title: How a qanat supports an agricultural settlement
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Groundwater in an alluvial aquifer"] -->|"Collected through"| B["Qanat tunnel"]
  B -->|"Conveyed by gravity to"| C["Surface outlet"]
  C -->|"Distributed through"| D["Irrigation channels"]
  D -->|"Supply water to"| E["Agricultural land"]
  F["Communal management"] -->|"Organizes sharing and maintenance"| B
  F -->|"Organizes water allocation"| D
```
content.summary: The diagram explains the water-delivery process and the distinct role of communal management described by UNESCO. It represents a historical settlement-support system, not a national map of current water supply.

content.heading: Distinguish temporary movement from permanent change
content.content:
Long-term settlement patterns can be disrupted by emergencies. In a March 2026 statement, UNHCR described preliminary evidence of temporary displacement from Tehran and other major urban areas toward northern and rural locations. That dated statement supports the existence and reported direction of emergency movement at that time; it does not establish how many people remained away at the October cutoff. [s7]

The distinction matters for interpreting human geography. A temporary destination is not automatically a new usual residence, and an emergency assessment should not be inserted into a census trend as though both measured the same population. A completed overview needs updated evidence on permanent settlement, return movements, provincial distribution, and border-city functions. Those gaps remain explicit here rather than being filled with unsupported contemporary claims.
